claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel spontaneously forms a nanometric passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film governs the early stages of corrosion in Q235 steel.
The integrity and defect density of the passive film determine whether localized pits nucleate.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxide-film formation on Q235 steel.
Accelerated oxide growth at elevated temperature produces a denser and more protective film.
The elevated-temperature oxide film suppresses pit initiation relative to room-temperature exposure.
Passive-film composition, thickness, and defect density modulate local electrochemical conditions.
At room temperature, film defects facilitate pit nucleation through localized pH and potential fluctuations.
A defect-reduced oxide film suppresses pit initiation.
Localized pitting begins earlier at room temperature than at elevated temperature.
Room-temperature samples exhibit higher corrosion current densities than elevated-temperature samples.
Elevated-temperature exposure produces a more uniform and stable oxide film.
Elevated-temperature samples exhibit delayed or reduced pit nucleation and lower corrosion current densities relative to the untreated reference.
Surface contaminants, alloying variation, and additional mechanical stresses could alter the proposed effects.

Temperature-controlled electrochemistry combined with time-resolved surface imaging, EIS, Tafel analysis, and XPS can measure film evolution, pit initiation, film resistance, corrosion current, composition, and defect density.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that groups experience identical thermal loads, but the intervention explicitly assigns room-temperature and elevated-temperature loads.

The predicted outcome asserts lower corrosion current at elevated temperature relative to the untreated reference, while the defined untreated reference is held in a non-corrosive inert environment and therefore is not an appropriate corrosive-current comparator.
